newsitem.title: UK: Brazil worried about forests as cocoa output falls.
newsitem.headline: Brazil worried about forests as cocoa output falls.

text.p: Brazil's tropical rainforests may come under threat as cocoa production dwindles and farmers no longer need shade for cocoa trees, a senior official said.

"Our farmers are angry...they are concerned about prices that don't reflect the fundamentals and their costs are higher," said Sergio Eduardo Moreira Lima, Minister-Counsellor at the Brazilian embassy in London.
"Now they see no reason to protect the tropical forests," Lima told Reuters during a International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) reception hosted by the Ivory Coast embassy.
In Bahia, Brazil's main cocoa growing area, many farmers frustrated about low world prices and the witches' broom disease that has ravaged the crop were selling their land for cattle grazing.
Commodity trade house E.D.& F. Man has forecast Brazil's 1996/97 output at a near 30-year low of 156,000 tonnes, down from 231,000 tonnes in 1995/96 due to extremely dry weather.
Lima said Brazil's presence in the world market was likely to diminish further as production continues to drop and domestic consumption increases.
Witches' broom has slashed production that had reached above 350,000 tonnes in 1990/91. The ICCO has put the 1996/97 crop at 195,000 tonnes.
Lima said the government was trying new strains to wipe out the disease from the fields but so far it had not been successful.

Brazil has been the main opponent to moves spearheaded by ICCO consumer countries to use the revenue from buffer stock sales, to which Brazil was the biggest contributor, for the liquidation of the existing international cocoa agreement and for administrative costs.
Brasilia has already allocated its share of an estimated $4 million profit from the sale of 250,000 tonnes of buffer stock cocoa to the fight against witches' broom, officials said.

Producer countries have tabled a new proposal on Wednesday to fund the liquidation separately from members' contributions -- an idea that angered consumers who are reluctant to see a spike in annual contributions.
"It's not acceptable. We don't see any logic behind it," said one consumer spokesman.
"All along we have said that buffer stock money was going to be used. Now suddenly things have taken a new turn," he added.
But Brazil, and other producers, were concerned about the legal aspect of channelling the buffer stock money to an entirely different purpose.
Producer and consumer camps will discuss the issue at an executive commitee meeting on Thursday but one delegate said there was "little scope" for agreement.
The issue has been on the ICCO agenda since December. A concensus is needed for an agreement.
